brand.subtitle: Knowledge Check — ESource WhiteLabel Sales Course

questions.question: What are the three main reasons that accounting firms buy the ESource white-label bookkeeping tool?
choices: Their brand, data stays home, and lower cost per client
Bank feeds, payroll integration, and client login portal
Mobile app, live bank feeds, and unlimited staff seats
Familiarity, ease of use, and built-in reporting
questions.feedback_correct: Exactly—these three reasons are the core value proposition and should be deliverable in one breath during any sales conversation.
questions.feedback_incorrect: The second and third options describe features the tool doesn't yet have or competitor strengths. The fourth option misses the strategic advantages that drive firm buying decisions.

questions.question: What is the ideal firm size (in monthly clients) that represents a great fit for this white-label tool?
choices: 1 to 5 clients
5 to 100 clients
100 to 500 clients
500+ clients
questions.feedback_correct: Right—bookkeeping and small CPA firms with roughly five to one hundred monthly clients are the sweet spot for this solution.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Firms smaller than five or much larger than one hundred typically have different needs or may not benefit as much from this positioning.

questions.question: During the demo, which feature should you show first to create the "moment that sells"?
choices: The bank statement upload with the Bank Check tab
The Ask Client feature with grouped questions
The firm-branded screen with their logo on the demo profile
The help assistant answering questions in plain English
questions.feedback_correct: Perfect—putting their logo on the demo profile ahead of time is explicitly called out as the moment that sells the firm-branding value.
questions.feedback_incorrect: While the other features are important parts of the demo, they come after the branded screen. The logo moment is the emotional anchor that resonates first.

questions.question: What is the proposed monthly cost for a firm with exactly 10 active client books?
choices: $140 per month
$150 per month
$173 per month
$200 per month
questions.feedback_correct: Correct—one client at $20 plus nine clients at $17 each equals $20 + $153 = $173 per month for ten clients.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Remember the pricing tiers are graduated: the first client is $20, then clients 2–10 are $17 each. Calculate at the firm's actual client count, not a flat rate.

questions.question: According to the course, what should you do before running any demo?
choices: Ask questions about their current tools, cost pain, brand visibility, and time spent on transactions
Show them the competitor comparison chart immediately
Display the firm-branded screen with their logo
Explain the pricing tiers and payment terms
questions.feedback_correct: Exactly—discovery questions uncover the pain first, and you'll repeat their own words back to them during the demo and close.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Jumping straight to the demo or pricing before discovery means you miss the chance to tailor your pitch to their specific frustrations and priorities.

questions.question: How should you respond to a prospect who says, "Our clients are very familiar with QuickBooks Online"?
choices: Tell them QuickBooks is outdated and they should switch immediately
Explain that clients get Excel reports with the firm's name and don't need to learn new software
Suggest they keep QuickBooks and use your tool as a backup system
Acknowledge that QuickBooks is better and offer a discount to win the deal
questions.feedback_correct: That's the right response—clients get reports branded with the firm's name, so they don't see or need to learn the underlying software.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Dismissing QuickBooks or suggesting the tool is secondary misses the point: clients care about the report quality and the firm's brand, not which software generated it.

questions.question: What is the key security story you should tell an owner who worries about employees leaving with client data?
choices: The tool uses military-grade encryption that no one can break
Only people the owner adds can sign in; when they leave, their access locks immediately, and even lost laptops stay unreadable
ESource monitors all user activity and alerts you to suspicious behavior
Client data is backed up to the cloud so you never lose it
questions.feedback_correct: Perfect—this is the owner's core concern, and the story reassures them that they retain complete control and their clients stay theirs.
questions.feedback_incorrect: The other options describe general security features but miss the specific human-control story that addresses the real fear: an employee walking out with client information.

questions.question: What should you propose when closing the deal, and why?
choices: Migrating all their clients immediately to prove the tool's reliability
A pilot of 3 to 5 clients for 60 days alongside their current system to reduce risk
A one-year contract with all their clients to lock in the discount
A free trial with no staff limits to show the full potential
questions.feedback_correct: Exactly—the pilot approach removes risk, allows them to measure success, and creates a natural path to scaling after the 60-day period.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A big switch or long commitment feels risky to the prospect. The pilot is how you build confidence and demonstrate value before they commit their full client base.

questions.question: When discussing pricing, why should you always use the phrase "proposed" rather than stating rates as final?
choices: To make the pricing sound flexible and negotiable
Because the pricing tiers are still being finalized and you should confirm with Joe before anything is signed
To leave room to offer a discount if they push back
To make the prospect feel like they're getting insider information
questions.feedback_correct: Correct—the pricing is still proposed, so saying "proposed" and confirming with Joe before signing protects both you and the prospect from confusion.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Using "proposed" is not a sales tactic but a compliance measure. The pricing hasn't been finalized, and misrepresenting it could create legal or trust issues.

questions.question: A prospect says, "We need live bank feeds to use this tool." How should you respond based on the course?
choices: Apologize and admit this is a major gap that makes the tool unsuitable for them
Explain that monthly downloads take minutes, every month ties to the bank, and many firms prefer this to feeds that can silently miss transactions
Offer to build live feeds for them as a custom feature at no extra cost
Suggest they use a third-party bank feed service instead
questions.feedback_correct: Well done—this response reframes the limitation as a benefit and builds confidence that the monthly reconciliation is robust and proven.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Apologizing or conceding the point weakens your position. The course teaches you to handle this objection honestly by highlighting why monthly proven reconciliation is actually an advantage.
